name: Bianca Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the dairy and the potatoes on my husband's family farm, Cobb's Hill. It's ninety cows in an old herringbone parlour, which is a milking shed where the cows stand at an angle in two rows, plus forty hectares of potatoes and some grass for silage. I'm in the parlour at five, then it's calves, then whatever the potatoes need, and I've got Dorota and a lad from the village under me in the busy months.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow by her face and her temper. Number 212 kicks if you come at her from the left, and I've known that for six years. What wears me out is that it's my father-in-law's farm and his name on everything, and I take a small wage. Luis, my husband, fixes lorries in town, and between us we cover the mortgage on our bungalow and not a lot more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. I've never used these AI things and I've managed fine. At the discussion group I'd say most of us were never going to change much anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means things stay as they are, and as they are is just about fine. Tight, but I know where I stand. I'd rather tight and familiar than something new I don't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep milking, keep the potatoes going, keep Walter, my father-in-law, from buying anything daft. If the milk price held, I might fix the parlour gates that have been tied up with baler twine for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you nervous even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price, always. One bad price review from the dairy and that's our margin gone for the year. AI has nothing to do with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you ever wish you had a bit more cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every month. We've usually got about two weeks' money in the account. When the washing machine went last spring, it went on the card and it's still there.

S0.say: I'm not surprised. I've never used these AI things and managed fine, and most of us farmers were never going to change much anyway.
S0.think: Things stay as they are, and that's just about fine. It's tight, but I know where I stand, and I'd rather tight and familiar than something I don't understand.
S0.do: Keeps milking and running the potatoes as usual and talks her father-in-law out of unnecessary purchases. Fixes the parlour gates if the milk price holds.
S0.quote: When the washing machine went last spring, it went on the card and it's still there.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is practical and plain-speaking, and her identity is tied to knowing each cow. Her worry in this picture is the milk price, not technology. She says outright that she prefers familiar hardship to unfamiliar change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say some farms will do well with robots and some won't, and that's how it's always been. I'd say it without getting worked up. People round here don't like a fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this one worries me. The Hendersons over the hill put in two milking robots last year, and now they milk two hundred cows with one man. If the dairy pays them more for steadier milk, we can't keep up with the old parlour, and Walter won't borrow at his age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back first: no holiday, no new car, maybe Sofia's riding lessons go. I'd wait and see how the Hendersons actually get on before I said a word about robots to Walter. I wouldn't be learning any of it myself, not yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like I've seen a bit of black cloud on the edge and I can't tell which way it's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for you to change your mind about the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing them work for three or four years without breaking the bank. And knowing who comes out at two in the morning when one breaks. That's what nobody tells you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis, first, at the kitchen table. Then maybe the vet, Dr Amadi, because she sees every farm and she'd tell me straight. I wouldn't ask anyone online.

S1.say: Some farms will do well with robots and some won't, and that's how it's always been. I'd say it without fuss, because people round here don't like one.
S1.think: This one worries me, because the neighbours milk two hundred cows with one man and two robots. If the dairy pays more for steady milk, our old parlour can't keep up, and Walter won't borrow at his age.
S1.do: Cuts the family holiday, puts off a new car and may stop her daughter's riding lessons. Waits to see how the neighbours' robots work out before raising it with her father-in-law and doesn't learn the technology herself.
S1.feel: Anxious, like seeing a dark cloud on the edge without knowing which way it's moving.
S1.quote: Seeing them work for three or four years without breaking the bank. And knowing who comes out at two in the morning when one breaks.
S1.fieldNote: Her public calm hides real worry, driven by a neighbour's robots she can see from her own fields. She doesn't oppose technology on principle; she wants years of proof and someone to call at night. She'd talk to her husband and the vet, never the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say very little in public. Maybe that it's a mess and nobody saw it coming. I'm not one for posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd finish us. If robots milk and harvest for nearly nothing, a farm like ours with an old parlour and no money to change is done in a year. Walter's seventy-one. I don't think he'd even try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Luis and Walter in the first week and talk about selling the herd while cows are still worth something. We'd cut everything back to the mortgage and food. I'd go to my sister in town to see if there's any work at the bakery where she is, and I'd ask the bank for time before we missed anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked. I feel it in my chest just saying it. It's like the whole thing's on ice and nobody can stand up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would selling the cows feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a funeral. I'd want to be there when the lorry came and I'd also want to be anywhere else. I'd keep 212 if I could, kicking and all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're all right and that the cows are going to a good farm. Sofia's eleven, she'd cry. Mateo's seven, he'd ask if we can keep the cat.

S2.say: I'd say very little in public, maybe that it's a mess nobody saw coming. I'm not one for posting things.
S2.think: It would finish us. A farm with an old parlour and no money to change is done in a year if robots milk and harvest for nearly nothing, and Walter's seventy-one and wouldn't try.
S2.do: Talks with her husband and father-in-law in the first week about selling the herd while cows still have value. Cuts spending to mortgage and food, asks her sister about bakery work and asks the bank for time before missing a payment.
S2.feel: Panicked, with a tightness in her chest, as if everything is on ice.
S2.quote: I'd want to be there when the lorry came and I'd also want to be anywhere else. I'd keep 212 if I could, kicking and all.
S2.fieldNote: Her public silence contrasts sharply with private panic. Selling the herd is the concrete fear, and she describes it as a funeral. Her plan leans on family, her sister and the bank, which fits her careful, unshowy outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is not long for a farm. You plan crops and cows years ahead. I'd say the government ought to help farms that can't afford the change, but I wouldn't be marching about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it's still bad, just slower. I'd be forty-eight, Walter would be seventy-six and probably passing the farm on. If it's Luis and me holding it with no money, I don't see how we'd buy what we'd need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put a bit aside every month, even fifty pounds, and get the washing machine off the card. I'd keep the herd for now and watch the prices. By year two or three, if things were clearly going the robot way, I'd talk about selling the cows and keeping the land for grass to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Better than the two-year one, but it sits on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to sell properly and not in a panic. That matters. But I still don't see myself learning to run robots at fifty, if I'm being honest with you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you prefer to wait and see. Is waiting the right thing here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. But every time I've rushed, it's cost us. I'd rather wait a year too long than sell a year too early.

S3.say: Five years isn't long for a farm, because we plan crops and cows years ahead. The government ought to help farms that can't afford the change, but I wouldn't be marching about it.
S3.think: It's still bad, just slower. I'd be 48, Walter would be passing the farm on, and with no money I don't see how Luis and I would buy what we'd need.
S3.do: Puts aside about fifty a month and clears the card debt. Keeps the herd while watching prices, and by year two or three considers selling the cows and renting out the land for grass if robots clearly take over.
S3.feel: Alarmed, less than in the two-year picture, but it weighs on her.
S3.quote: I'd rather wait a year too long than sell a year too early.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her time for an orderly exit, not a transformation; she's frank that she won't learn robots at fifty. Her caution comes from experience of rushing and losing. She still expects to leave dairying, just not in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for young ones to find something else and for older ones to see out their time. I'd say farms shouldn't be pushed out, but nobody can stop progress either. That's about as far as I'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is the one I can live with. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and the farm would be Luis's to decide on. I'd still be anxious, but it's not my house on the line overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep milking and save what I could. I'd talk to Sofia about what she wants to do, and I'd tell her not to take on the farm unless she really loves it. Maybe in five years I'd look at the robots again, if the Hendersons were still happy with theirs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, still. But it's a slow anxious, not a fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you consider doing something other than farming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it, but there's not much round here. Maybe the feed merchants or the vet's office. I've never worked anywhere but a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people to know about farms like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're not stupid for being careful. When you've got two weeks' money in the bank, careful is the only way to stay standing.

S4.say: Ten years is enough for young ones to find something else and older ones to see out their time. Farms shouldn't be pushed out, but nobody can stop progress either.
S4.think: Ten years is the one I can live with. I'd be 53, the kids would be grown and the farm would be Luis's to decide on, so it's not my house on the line overnight.
S4.do: Keeps milking and saves what she can. Talks with her daughter about her future and tells her not to take on the farm unless she loves it, and might revisit milking robots in about five years if the neighbours are still happy with theirs.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but slowly rather than suddenly.
S4.quote: When you've got two weeks' money in the bank, careful is the only way to stay standing.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she settles into a slow, manageable worry and hands the bigger decisions to the next generation. She might consider robots in five years, but only on the neighbours' proof. Her defence of being careful is the clearest statement of her whole outlook.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Selling the cows in a panic would break my heart and our bank account at the same time. What would help is time, really, and some help for small farms to either change or get out with something left.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the old people. Walter's done fifty years on that hill. Nobody's got a plan for a seventy-year-old farmer who can't use a phone, never mind a robot.

headlineQuote: Nobody's got a plan for a seventy-year-old farmer who can't use a phone, never mind a robot.
portrait: Bianca Reyes is a 43-year-old who runs the dairy herd and potatoes on her husband's family farm, knows every cow by temper, and has never used an AI tool. She draws a small wage, her husband fixes lorries, and they have about two weeks of money in the bank. She's calm in the hype picture but anxious about steady change because a neighbour's milking robots already show what's coming. A two-year AGI arrival would mean selling the herd in a panic, while five or ten years let her plan a slower, orderly exit and leave the big choices to the next generation.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because they'd have to sell the cows in a panic and lose both the herd and their money.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and help for small farms to either change or leave with something left.
